questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'I think she ___ the exam next month.'
questions.context: A student makes a prediction about the coming year.

options.text: will pass
options.feedback: Correct. 'Will' plus the base form expresses a prediction or opinion about a future situation.

options.text: is passing
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is passing' is present continuous, which refers to something already arranged but not to a prediction.

options.text: passed
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Passed' is the past simple and cannot describe a future event.

options.text: passes
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Passes' is present simple and would state a fact about the present moment.

questions.explanation:
A prediction about what will probably happen is expressed with will plus the base form, which carries no commitment.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly expresses a prediction based on visible evidence.
questions.context: A speaker bases a prediction on present evidence.

options.text: Look at those clouds; it is going to rains.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Rains' after 'going to' is wrong; the infinitive after 'to' must stay in its base form.

options.text: Look at those clouds; it is going to rain.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Is going to' signals a prediction drawn from present evidence rather than a spontaneous opinion.

options.text: Look at those clouds; it goes to rain.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Goes to rain' is not a standard construction; the future forms are will and be going to.

options.text: Look at those clouds; it will rains.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will' is followed directly by the base form, so an -s ending cannot appear there.

questions.explanation:
The difference between will and be going to lies in the evidence behind the prediction, and the presence of clouds points clearly to be going to.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that reports an intention decided in advance.
questions.context: Two friends discuss weekend plans.

options.text: I visited my aunt this weekend.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Visited' is past simple and describes a completed action.

options.text: I visit my aunt this weekend.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Visit' is present simple and would describe a repeated or general action.

options.text: I'm going to visit my aunt this weekend.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Am going to' states a prior intention or plan, which is the standard use of this future form.

options.text: I am visit my aunt this weekend.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Am visit' lacks the infinitive after 'to'.

questions.explanation:
An intention formed before the moment of speaking is expressed with be going to, as opposed to will, which tends to be more spontaneous.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that expresses a spontaneous decision made at the moment of speaking.
questions.context: A traveller makes an instant decision at the airport.

options.text: I took the window seat.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Took' is past simple and places the decision in the past.

options.text: I take the window seat.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Take' is present simple and expresses a habit or a general fact.

options.text: I'm taking the window seat.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I'm taking' states an intention or arrangement decided earlier, not an instant choice.

options.text: I'll take the window seat.
options.feedback: Correct. 'I'll' is typical for a decision taken spontaneously in the act of speaking.

questions.explanation:
English contrasts a decision made at the moment of speaking, which uses will, with an intention formed earlier, which uses be going to.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the future perfect sentence.
questions.context: A speaker discusses something completed before a future point.

options.text: By December I will have finished the thesis.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Will have finished' shows the action completed before the future reference point of December.

options.text: By December I finish the thesis.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Finish' is the base form and cannot convey a future relationship.

options.text: By December I am finishing the thesis.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Am finishing' is present continuous and belongs to the present period.

options.text: By December I will finish the thesis.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will finish' is the future simple, which presents December as the moment of completion rather than the deadline.

questions.explanation:
The future perfect looks back from a future point, so it is the natural form after expressions such as 'by' plus a future date.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the future continuous sentence.
questions.context: A speaker describes an action that will be under way at a future moment.

options.text: At nine tonight we will waiting for the results.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will waiting' omits the second part of the auxiliary that the continuous requires.

options.text: At nine tonight we will be waiting for the results.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Will be' plus the gerund is the future continuous and marks an activity in progress at a stated future moment.

options.text: At nine tonight we will be wait for the results.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will be wait' uses the base form where the gerund is required.

options.text: At nine tonight we will waits for the results.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will waits' keeps the third person -s ending, which cannot follow a modal auxiliary.

questions.explanation:
The future continuous is formed with will be plus the gerund, and it marks an action as under way at a particular point in the future.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement correctly explains the difference between will and be going to?
questions.context: An exam asks the learner to distinguish the two basic future forms.

options.text: Will is used for predictions and be going to is used for past events.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Be going to' has no use with past events; it is exclusively a future form.

options.text: Be going to is used for spontaneous decisions, while will is used only for past habits.
options.feedback: Wrong. It reverses the usual distribution and omits predictions, promises and habits from the explanation.

options.text: Be going to is used for intentions and evidence-based predictions, while will is used for spontaneous decisions, promises and neutral predictions.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the standard distinction, and it explains the choice on the basis of intention, evidence and spontaneity.

options.text: Both forms are interchangeable in all contexts without any difference in meaning.
options.feedback: Wrong. The two forms differ in meaning, so they are not freely interchangeable.

questions.explanation:
A reliable explanation of a future contrast rests on the speaker's intention or the evidence available at the moment of speaking.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly predicts something with a numerical estimate.
questions.context: A coach corrects a habit statement in the future.

options.text: The population will doubled in twenty years.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will doubled' places a past participle after a modal auxiliary, which is not a valid form.

options.text: The population will be doubling in twenty years.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will be doubling' describes an activity under way at a future moment rather than a total change.

options.text: The population is going to doubles in twenty years.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Going to doubles' wrongly inflects the infinitive that follows 'to'.

options.text: The population will double in twenty years.
options.feedback: Correct. A prediction supported by an estimate uses will plus the base form in its neutral sense.

questions.explanation:
When a speaker bases a prediction on a calculation rather than on a decision or visible evidence, will is the neutral and accurate choice.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that reports an action completed before a future deadline.
questions.context: A project plan reports progress at a future deadline.

options.text: By the end of the term, we will have submitted every report.
options.feedback: Correct. The future perfect presents each report as finished before the deadline named in the opening phrase.

options.text: By the end of the term, we will submitted every report.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will submitted' is not a valid modal form; modals are followed by the base form or the infinitive.

options.text: By the end of the term, we will be submitting every report.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will be submitting' describes the activity at the deadline rather than its completion before it.

options.text: By the end of the term, we will have submit every report.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Have submit' lacks the past participle that the future perfect requires.

questions.explanation:
Project reporting about a deadline usually prefers the future perfect because it emphasises completion strictly before the named moment.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that describes an activity already planned for a future moment.
questions.context: A speaker looks forward to a fixed future moment.

options.text: This time next year we will being living in Bogotá.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will being' omits the auxiliary that the future continuous requires after 'will'.

options.text: This time next year we will be living in Bogotá.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Will be living' describes the situation as already established when next year arrives.

options.text: This time next year we live in Bogotá.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Live' is present simple and states the current situation rather than the future one.

options.text: This time next year we will lives in Bogotá.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will lives' keeps the third person ending that cannot follow a modal.

questions.explanation:
A fixed future time expression such as 'this time next year' is often paired with the future continuous to show the situation as already arranged.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that is typical for a spontaneous promise.
questions.context: A speaker offers a promise at the moment of speaking.

options.text: I send you the notes tonight, I promise.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I send' is present simple and does not express a commitment about the future.

options.text: I'm going to send you the notes tonight, I promise.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I'm going to send' states a pre-existing intention, so it is less appropriate for an instant promise.

options.text: I'll send you the notes tonight, I promise.
options.feedback: Correct. 'I'll' is the conventional form for a promise offered spontaneously during the conversation.

options.text: I sent you the notes tonight, I promise.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I sent' is past simple and claims the notes have already been sent.

questions.explanation:
Promises made at the moment of speaking are strongly associated with will, which carries the sense of commitment at that instant.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which explanation of the future perfect is correct?
questions.context: A time diagram is used to explain a future perfect.

options.text: It shows an action whose time of occurrence is deliberately left unspecified.
options.feedback: Wrong. Leaving the time unspecified is the function of the present perfect, which links past and present.

options.text: It shows an action that happened before another past action.
options.feedback: Wrong. That description corresponds to the past perfect, not the future perfect.

options.text: It shows an action still continuing at the moment of speaking.
options.feedback: Wrong. An action still continuing at the present is described by the present continuous.

options.text: It shows an action as complete before a future reference point in the sentence.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the defining function of the future perfect, which looks back from a point in the future.

questions.explanation:
Each perfect form has a distinct anchor: the present perfect looks from now, the past perfect from a past point and the future perfect from a future one.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the negative future perfect sentence.
questions.context: An exam tests the negative form of the future perfect.

options.text: By then she won't have finished the translation.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Won't' plus 'have' plus the past participle forms the negative future perfect and contracts naturally in speech.

options.text: By then she haven't finished the translation.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Haven't' is the present perfect and does not agree with the singular subject in any case.

options.text: By then she isn't finishing the translation.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Isn't finishing' is negative present continuous and has no future anchor.

options.text: By then she won't have finish the translation.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Won't have finish' lacks the past participle that 'have' requires.

questions.explanation:
The negative of the future perfect negates the modal, so 'will not' plus 'have' plus participle is the structure to use.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly predicts a repeated future habit.
questions.context: A speaker discusses a habit projected into the future.

options.text: People will uses bicycles more in the cities of the future.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will uses' adds a third person ending that cannot appear after a modal auxiliary.

options.text: People will use bicycles more in the cities of the future.
options.feedback: Correct. A prediction about a general future tendency takes will plus the base form with no inflection on the verb.

options.text: People will be use bicycles more in the cities of the future.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will be use' uses the base form after 'be' in the continuous position, which requires a gerund.

options.text: People will used bicycles more in the cities of the future.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will used' places a past form after a modal, which is not a valid combination.

questions.explanation:
Modal auxiliaries are followed by the base form, never by an -s or -ed ending, which is the structural point being tested here.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that shows a decision taken because of present circumstances.
questions.context: A speaker justifies a decision made from current evidence.

options.text: The roads are blocked, so we are take the train.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are take' lacks the infinitive that must follow 'to'.

options.text: The roads are blocked, so we'll take the train.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'We'll' reads as a spontaneous decision made at the moment of speaking, without the evidential basis.

options.text: The roads are blocked, so we're going to take the train.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Are going to' presents the choice as based on visible current evidence, which is its normal use.

options.text: The roads are blocked, so we will took the train.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will took' places a past form after a modal auxiliary, which is not valid.

questions.explanation:
Be going to is appropriate when the reason for the decision is visible or measurable at the time of speaking.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which 'be going to' is used exactly as the examination expects.
questions.context: A comparison item contrasts two future forms.

options.text: The volcano is to erupt; scientists say the pressure keeps rising.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is to erupt' expresses an arrangement rather than a prediction drawn from evidence.

options.text: The volcano is going to erupt; scientists say the pressure has kept rising.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has kept rising' refers to a completed interval up to now, which removes the sense of a developing trend.

options.text: The volcano will erupting; scientists say the pressure keeps rising.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will erupting' combines a modal with a gerund, which is not a valid future construction.

options.text: The volcano is going to erupt; scientists say the pressure keeps rising.
options.feedback: Correct. Present evidence of rising pressure supports the predictive use of 'is going to' before the verb 'erupt'.

questions.explanation:
The item tests whether the learner matches the future form to the type of evidence cited in the second clause.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly describes the process continuing into the future period.
questions.context: A researcher writes about a long-running process that will still be active in the future.

options.text: Urban migration continues, and it will continue well beyond 2050.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Will continue' is the plain future form and correctly predicts that the process carries on past that date.

options.text: Urban migration continues, and it will continues well beyond 2050.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will continues' adds a third person ending after the modal, which is grammatically incorrect.

options.text: Urban migration continues, and it will being well beyond 2050.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will being' is not a valid future form; the continuous requires 'will be continuing'.

options.text: Urban migration continues, and it will be continued well beyond 2050.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will be continued' is the passive and suggests an external agent restarts the process rather than its ongoing continuation.

questions.explanation:
When a process that already exists is projected forward unchanged, the plain future form is the accurate and simplest option.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which revision best fits a formal forecast about a completed action before a deadline?
questions.context: An editing task evaluates an informal plan in a formal document.

options.text: By the close of the fiscal year the department will reduce its expenditure by a fifth.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will reduce' places the reduction at the deadline and leaves completion before it unmarked.

options.text: By the close of the fiscal year the department will have reduced its expenditure by a fifth.
options.feedback: Correct. In a formal forecast the future perfect stresses that the reduction will be complete before the deadline rather than at it.

options.text: By the close of the fiscal year the department reduces its expenditure by a fifth.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Reduces' is present simple and contradicts the future framing of the sentence.

options.text: By the close of the fiscal year the department is reducing its expenditure by a fifth.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is reducing' refers to the present period and cannot be placed under a future deadline.

questions.explanation:
Formal forecasting language prefers the future perfect when the document needs to guarantee completion strictly before the stated deadline.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which all three future forms are correct and each contributes a distinct meaning.
questions.context: An exam item tests three future forms within a single narrative.

options.text: By 2030 the company will have opened six branches, and it is expanding into Asia next year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is expanding' is present continuous and would require a present reference point rather than next year.

options.text: By 2030 the company will have opened six branches, and it expands into Asia next year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'It expands' is present simple and cannot carry the projection into next year.

options.text: By 2030 the company will have opened six branches, and it will expand into Asia next year.
options.feedback: Correct. The future perfect gives the completed position at 2030 and the future simple gives the projected next move, with no overlap in meaning.

options.text: By 2030 the company will has opened six branches, and it will expand into Asia next year.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will has opened' combines a modal with a perfect auxiliary, which is not a valid combination in standard English.

questions.explanation:
Examinations reward the ability to combine future forms so that each one carries its own distinct temporal contribution.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence makes the strongest and least open-ended promise?
questions.context: A classroom task asks the learner to identify an overconfident commitment.

options.text: The committee will have announced the results tomorrow, and the decision depends on the final count.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will have announced' places the announcement before the reference point and 'depends on the final count' removes the commitment.

options.text: The committee will be announcing the results tomorrow, and the decision is under discussion.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will be announcing' implies an ongoing process and 'under discussion' signals that nothing is settled.

options.text: The committee might announce the results tomorrow, and the decision is open to review.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Might' introduces uncertainty and 'open to review' explicitly keeps the decision provisional.

options.text: The committee will announce the results tomorrow, and the decision is final.
options.feedback: Correct. This combines an unqualified future commitment with an explicit statement that the outcome is settled.

questions.explanation: A strong promise requires an unqualified future form together with wording that explicitly excludes any possibility of change.
questions.subject: ingles
